title: Why is it so hard to say "toy boat" three times fast?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why "toy boat" is hard to say three times fast. They cover tongue twisters across languages (Japanese examples, a Chinese one), phonological disorders and their causes (structural, neurological, indeterminate), the lingual frenulum, the motor theory of speech perception (Liberman) and the Haber study on silently reading tongue twisters, the "six sheeps sick" tongue twister, spoonerisms, finger fumblers in sign language, and the finding that average speakers make about one error per thousand words. The episode closes with listener mail from Laila Feldman about green burial traditions, following up on a prior episode on what to do with the dead body.

segments.title: Opening banter and toy boat challenge
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter, then try saying 'toy boat' three times fast. They note Jerry does it easily and that tongue twisters are found in many languages.

segments.title: Tongue twisters in other languages
segments.summary: Chuck asks for foreign tongue twisters. Josh shares a Chinese example and two Japanese ones, with translations, noting that tongue twisters often do not translate into English tongue twisters.

segments.title: Phonological disorders and speech development
segments.summary: Josh explains phonological disorders as failure to develop correct pronunciation of phonemes. Examples include dropping the -ing ending, and the hosts note that 7 to 10 percent of five-year-olds have one. They describe mild and severe forms and the three causes: structural, neurological, and indeterminate origin.

segments.title: The tongue and the lingual frenulum
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the lingual frenulum, the tissue tying the tongue to the floor of the mouth. A frenulum that is too short can cause a speech impediment, and surgery can correct it.

segments.title: Motor theory of speech and the Haber study
segments.summary: Josh describes Al Liberman's 1960s motor theory of speech perception, which holds that we hear speech using the same brain areas we use to produce it. He then describes the Haber study, in which college-aged subjects took longer to silently read tongue-twister sentences than control sentences, which supports the theory. Chuck mentions the six sheeps sick tongue twister and the hosts discuss spoonerisms and sign language finger fumblers.

segments.title: Why toy boat is hard and speech error rates
segments.summary: The hosts say there is no definitive answer for why 'toy boat' is hard, whether physical (tongue movement) or a brain issue. The average speaker makes about one error per thousand words.

segments.title: Listener mail on green burial
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck read listener mail from Laila Feldman, who says the recent dead-body episode left out older traditional burial practices, such as Jewish shroud burial, pine boxes, and the Roman and Turkish practice of reburying bones. The hosts sign off with a reminder to email and visit the website.
